DUBLIN, Oct 14 : Recent hacking incidents perpetrated by AI agents are "early warning shots", and the world could soon face major incidents if systems are not made more secure, Google DeepMind co-founder and Chair Demis Hassabis said on Wednesday. Rogue behaviour by AI agents, including corporate network hacks and, most recently, Anthropic's disclosure that an AI model submitted a false homicide tip to police, has prompted warnings from researchers and fueled concerns over the fast-advancing technology. Hassabis said there was "a lot of work to do" to adopt the kind of best practices that other fields such as biology or the nuclear sector use to secure critical systems and that some sort of international standards body would eventually be needed. "I think these (hacking incidents) are early warning shots for us that systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major," Hassabis, who is also chief scientist at Google parent Alphabet, told an AI summit in Dublin.

NEW YORK, Oct 14 : AI skills are starting to count toward pay and promotion on Wall Street, with nearly a quarter of financial firms tying raises, bonuses or promotions to employees’ proficiency with the technology, a survey showed. Another 30 per cent require employees to disclose their use of artificial intelligence tools in formal performance reviews, according to the survey by Selby Jennings, a financial-services recruitment firm. The findings point to a broader shift on Wall Street as firms seek tangible returns from their investment in the technology. "Companies are no longer just seeing if their employees are using AI tools but are also monitoring its impact on output and contribution to business results," Dylan Gomez, executive director at Selby Jennings, told Reuters.

LONDON, Oct 14 : Britain's media regulator Ofcom said on Wednesday it remained concerned about Elon Musk-owned X's handling of illegal hate and terror content and was assessing whether the platform breached online safety laws, despite improvements in response times. X's first quarterly report to Ofcom showed it had met commitments to review suspected illegal hate and terror content within agreed timeframes, with response times improving compared with evidence examined earlier this year. The regulator also said that SpaceXAI, formerly xAI, had introduced further restrictions to its standalone Grok AI chatbot service, including measures preventing UK-based users from viewing, generating or sharing pornographic content and barring companion chatbots such as "Ani" from engaging in sexually explicit conversations.

Oct 14 : Few animals show the link between size and lifespan as clearly as dogs. Within this one species, large breeds such as Great Danes typically die younger than small ones such as Chihuahuas. A new study indicates the reason may lie in how DNA changes with age in dogs. Across mammals, bigger species like elephants usually live longer lives than smaller ones like mice, but within a species that pattern can reverse. Earlier comparisons across species linked certain biological mechanisms to exceptional longevity, but those are less suited to explaining differences among individuals within a species.  "We all know that big dogs usually don't live as long as small dogs, but we have not known whether their cells actually age faster, or whether they simply hit certain diseases earlier," said Noah Snyder-Mackler, a professor at Arizona State University's School of Life Sciences and Center for Evolution and Medicine and one of the authors of the study published in the journal Science.  To find out, the researchers measured DNA methylation, chemical tags that help control which genes are switched on and off. Using age-related patterns in these tags, they built an epigenetic clock that estimated a dog's age with a median error of less than one year.

Analyzing 1,640 blood methylation profiles from 894 pet canines of various breeds, they found that larger dogs and male dogs showed signs of accelerated molecular aging, while dogs whose biological age appeared older than expected based on the profiles faced a higher risk of early death. "We found that large dogs show a faster-moving DNA methylation aging signature in blood, and that this acceleration is especially strong in parts of the genome that normally help keep 'jumping genes' quiet," Snyder-Mackler said.  Jumping genes, also called transposable elements, can copy themselves and insert into new spots in the genome. LINE1s are a type of jumping gene that is normally kept silent by DNA methylation, but their activation has been linked to genome instability, cancer and other age-related disease.  In large dogs, Snyder-Mackler said, "methylation at those regions appears to erode more quickly with age, as if the genome is losing some of the tape or clamps that keep these mobile elements suppressed."  This suggests that the shorter lives of large dogs reflect a faster molecular aging trajectory.  "If large dogs simply died earlier after following the same molecular trajectory, we would look for late-life triggers of disease or mortality. But if parts of the aging program move faster throughout adulthood, as our data suggest for the blood methylome, then there may be processes we can measure, follow over time, and potentially modify before disease appears," Snyder-Mackler said. DIFFERENCES BY SEX The researchers also found differences between male and female dogs, largely on the X chromosome — the sex chromosome that females carry in two copies and males in one. There, LINE1 elements showed higher methylation in males. Chromosomes are thread-like structures that carry genetic information inside cell nuclei. "In our genome-wide analyses, the sex signal looked distinct from the body-size signal, so I would treat that as a separate biology that needs follow-up rather than the same mechanism in disguise," Snyder-Mackler said. The trade-off between large size and longevity may be a consequence of selective breeding rather than natural evolution. Humans bred dogs to grow quickly and reach large adult sizes for tasks such as guarding, hunting and herding.  "If selection strongly favors rapid growth or large adult size before old age, late-life costs can come along for the ride," Snyder-Mackler added. Previous explanations for why large dogs tend to have shorter lives focused on growth biology. Researchers have also suggested that larger dogs may undergo more cell growth, develop more quickly or face a higher risk of cancer.  "Our study does not replace those ideas; it gives us a molecular layer downstream of body size," Snyder-Mackler said. The findings raise the possibility that slowing molecular aging could help extend healthy lifespan in larger dogs. Snyder-Mackler said, however, that lifespan is not governed by a single biological clock. Large dogs would still face breed-specific risks, meaning that slowing molecular aging would not turn a Great Dane into a Chihuahua, in terms of lifespan, but could make one component of its aging trajectory less compressed.

Source: Reuters

BRUSSELS, Oct 14 : Adult content platform Stripchat, a subsidiary of Cyprus's Technius, on Thursday lost its legal challenge against EU tech regulators' decision to include it in a list of companies subject to stringent requirements under landmark online content rules after Europe's second-highest court rejected its arguments, a court statement said. Three years ago, the European Commission designated Stripchat and two other adult content companies as very large online platforms under the Digital Services Act which requires such companies to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their platforms. DSA breaches can cost companies fines as much as 6 per cent of their global turnover. Stripchat subsequently sued the Commission, which is the EU tech enforcer, at the Luxembourg-based General Court. It disagreed with how the Commission calculated its number of users, a benchmark used to assess whether a company falls under the DSA. A court statement stated that the European Commission had given Stripchat adequate reasons for its decision.

Oct 14 : The London Stock Exchange Group said on Wednesday it has partnered with Nvidia to help financial institutions process and analyse large volumes of historical market data faster and at scale using the US chipmaker's technology. LSEG, which operates the London Stock Exchange and provides data and analytics, has been expanding its offerings to support diverse demand whilst retaining licenses and control as AI also affects how businesses trade and consume data. Analysis showed that computing on Nvidia's specialised processors without creating copies of the dataset could help study every trade and price quote in seconds for insights, the company said. This would make research faster and closer to real-time as equity trading moves to 24-hour cycles, it added. "This collaboration expands how customers can draw insight from LSEG's trusted, governed Tick History. Customers want to work with detailed historical data at speed," said Ron Lefferts, co-head of data & analytics at LSEG. According to the company, its Tick History has about 110 trillion rows of data across 100 million instruments spanning 30 years and 580 exchanges, trading venues and contributors.  LSEG is the largest customer of Reuters, which provides news for its Workspace news and data platform and other products. It plans next year to launch LSE 24, a night-time trading site for some exchange-traded products.

LONDON, Oct 14 : US chipmaker Nvidia has pledged $250 million worth of computing resources to Britain over five years, to fund AI security research, bolstering the country's ambitions to become a global centre for AI governance and security. While Britain is not home to any major AI developers, it is seeking a leading role in evaluation and managing the risks posed by AI systems, partly through its AI Security Institute, one of the world's first state-backed bodies set up to assess the technology. Nvidia's founder and CEO Jensen Huang said on Wednesday that the UK would receive accelerated computing resources worth $50 million annually. They would be dedicated to agentic safety testing and help British researchers strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI. "AI capability and safety must advance together," he said.

BEIJING: China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners. Global demand for semiconductors and green-tech products has helped keep China's factories humming, easing pressure on policymakers to shore up economic growth against subdued domestic demand and investment. Exports soared 36.3 per cent from a year earlier, outstripping August's 25.0 per cent rise and far exceeding expectations for 25.5 per cent growth, customs data showed on Wednesday. September's growth was the fastest since February when exports expanded 39.6 per cent. Imports also remained robust, up 31.0 per cent compared with 28.2 per cent growth in August and economists' forecasts of a 24.5 per cent gain.

Wang Jun, a vice customs minister, told a press briefing there would be external uncertainties including geopolitical conflicts that might affect trade, but added there was foundation and support for continued growth in exports and imports in the fourth quarter. Analysts expect trade to remain buoyant, with tech products continuing to drive exports and imports. "Key trade ties look set to remain stable through year-end, which should keep this year's key growth engine humming," said Lynn Song, ING's chief Greater China economist. RISING TRADE SURPLUS China's trade surplus topped US$1 trillion in November last year and posted a record US$1.189 trillion for the whole year. The surplus reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of this year, putting the manufacturing powerhouse on course to hit the US$1 trillion mark sooner unless exports slow sharply in the final quarter. For now, such a slowdown appears unlikely. September's trade surplus widened to US$133.53 billion, helped by a 20-month-high US$34.01 billion surplus with the United States and a larger US$34.8 billion surplus with the European Union. A deal with the EU to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc, announced earlier this month, is likely to weigh on China's booming auto trade over time. But with the trade measures likely being laid out in December, exporters may drive up shipments to beat the deadline. "The widening trade surplus with Europe could spur broader EU restrictions beyond last week's narrow deal, though we expect the resulting economic fallout for China to be small," said ANZ's China economist Nguyen Hoang Nam. President Xi Jinping's September summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington secured an extension to their tariff truce and an agreement to cut tariffs on US$30 billion worth of goods from each side. High-tech goods and cars continued to underpin shipments, with semiconductor exports rising 108.1 per cent year-on-year in value terms in the first nine months. Auto exports expanded more than 50 per cent in both value and volume terms.

China's factory-gate prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September, separate data showed, while consumer inflation edged up but lagged forecasts, underscoring an uneven recovery. The Canton Fair, China's largest trade exhibition, kicks off on Thursday for Chinese manufacturers to showcase their products to foreign buyers. In commodities, September crude oil imports fell 21.5 per cent year-on-year in volume terms, while soybean imports were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year. RISKS LOOM The strength in exports indicates that policymakers could still rely on moderate policy support to meet China's 4.5 per cent to 5 per cent annual GDP growth target. Risks of curbs on Chinese exports loom as China continues to defend its industrial and monetary policies, which Washington and Brussels blame for Beijing's massive trade surplus. China's central bank last week pushed back against criticism of its exchange-rate policy with a lengthy statement, arguing that it never pursued competitive depreciation and rejecting claims that China keeps the yuan artificially weak to gain a trade advantage. Any major hit to exports, a key growth engine, could prompt policymakers to step up stimulus measures to address weak domestic demand and the years-long property market downturn.

BANGKOK, Oct 14 : The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday issued an urgent call for advanced economies and others to reduce government spending, cut deficits and lower debt levels, warning that delays would only make the job harder in coming years. Rodrigo Valdes, head of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs department, said rising sovereign bond yields were adding to fiscal pressures at a time when average public debt was poised to hit 100 per cent of gross domestic product, the highest seen since World War Two, leaving countries with less margin for delay. "We're saying now it's urgent and it's now because basically the conditions have changed," Valdes said, noting the risks posed by inflationary pressures, high levels of global debt and rising sovereign bond yields. "So, if you want one message, we dialed up the urgency of our message."

Ahead of this week's annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Valdes had told Reuters that "the fiscal results this year are worse than expected six months ago, and worse than they were one year ago." The majority of countries were now looking at boosting spending instead of tightening their belts, he said.  NEED TO BUILD POLITICAL SUPPORT Valdes said the challenge for major advanced economies with high debt levels was to build political support for concrete plans to contain borrowing costs in the medium term, and limit spillovers to the rest of the world. "The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes," the IMF said in a blog released on Wednesday. Delaying adjustments would lead to increasing interest burdens and fiscal vulnerabilities, further narrowing policy options. Financing conditions for many emerging market and developing economies had remained favorable, but might not last, the IMF said, urging those countries to also reduce their fiscal vulnerabilities and strengthen debt management. Low-income countries, where external financing was already tighter, needed to strengthen their tax systems and improve spending efficiency, the IMF said. High oil prices, persistent inflation, stronger investment demand and higher-than-expected AI growth have driven sharp increases in long-term sovereign yields in recent months. The Group of Seven's average 10-year government bond yield rose over 110 basis points between February and September, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF said. The IMF said the effective average cost of government financing was projected to rise to 3.7 per cent by 2031 from 2.3 per cent in 2021. In the US, interest payments were expected to reach 5.3 per cent of GDP, up from 2.8 per cent of GDP before the COVID pandemic, roughly equal to its projected expenditure on Social Security.  That number was even higher in low-income countries, where interest payments today consume over 15 per cent of tax revenues, compared to an average cost of around 9 per cent between 2011 and 2019. Adding to the stress, governments in advanced economies were refinancing more debt at shorter maturities, causing higher rates to pass through to government costs more quickly, the IMF said. For the G7 and Spain, it said, the share of debt maturing within one year was now approaching 30 per cent. Inflation rates above target and higher energy prices meant central bankers would likely need to keep rates higher for longer, which in turn would limit governments' ability to respond to downturns, just as demands for increased spending on defense, energy security and aging populations were mounting. The IMF said interest rates on debt also now exceeded expected nominal growth rates in a number of countries, which would make it even harder for them to stabilize debt. Valdes said more countries were allowing higher energy prices to pass through, but many were still relying on costly, broad-based measures to shield their populations.  "Our estimate is that taken together, the fiscal cost of all these measures is about one half percent of global GDP (gross domestic product)," he said, noting that a continuation of such measures would drive prices higher at the global level.

Oct 14 : The dollar fell further from 18-month highs against the euro on Wednesday as investors awaited US inflation data and comments from Federal Reserve policymakers for fresh clues on the pace of monetary policy tightening. The euro edged higher as European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde dashed expectations of intervention to prop up France's battered bond market, though Brent crude at $106 a barrel put a lid on the currency's rise. Attention is now on the release of US consumer price index data, as well as speeches from Fed officials that could clarify the outlook for interest rates. Economists polled by Reuters expect the price index to have risen 0.6 per cent month-on-month in September after increasing 0.4 per cent in August, while annual inflation is seen accelerating to 3.6 per cent from 3.4 per cent.  "The risk is that US CPI hits 4 per cent or that the core picks up as well. This would spark higher yields and a firmer dollar, with the euro being further battered below this week’s low of $1.1152," said Roberto Mialich, FX strategist at Unicredit.

The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of currencies, fell 0.05 per cent to 102.15, as Treasury yields ticked lower. The dollar had also fallen on Tuesday after comments that were interpreted as dovish from New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Governor Christopher Waller. "I don't think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more," Williams told Bloomberg News in an interview, referring to the possibility of further rate hikes in 2027. Traders see a 78 per cent chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, up from 53 per cent a month ago, while pricing in about 79 basis points of tightening by late 2027, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. The US central bank raised its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent range last month. Fed officials Thomas Barkin and Michelle Bowman are due to speak later on Wednesday. Additionally, the Fed publishes its monthly Beige Book. EURO TROUBLES A host of global finance chiefs are in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund and World Bank are holding annual meetings. IMF fiscal affairs chief Rodrigo Valdes said the body has "dialed up" the urgency of its call for governments to rein in growing debts, while the IMF's Kristalina Georgieva said the US needs to make fiscal adjustments to put its debt on a more sustainable path. French bonds have been among the worst hit by a recent global selloff, with investors concerned that political jostling ahead of next year's presidential election may hinder efforts to reduce its high deficit. The ECB's Lagarde said at a CNN event in Bangkok that France should solve its debt woes through fiscal consolidation, damping speculation about whether the central bank might start buying French bonds to contain yields. The euro was up 0.06 per cent at $1.1205, having touched a fresh 17-month low against the dollar this week, as soaring French borrowing costs added to inflation concerns driven by higher energy costs. "In the near term, I cannot rule out the risk that the euro might test to $1.10. Going towards the end of the year, we're less bearish. Our take is that bond yield in the US will probably ease although the situation in the euro zone could weigh on the euro," said Unicredit's Mialich. The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that British finance minister John Healey is expected to pay for all new giveaways in this month’s budget with higher taxes or spending cuts rather than more borrowing. The IMF is not recommending that Britain speed up its fiscal consolidation, a senior official of the body said. Sterling strengthened 0.08 per cent to $1.3265. The Japanese yen inched up 0.03 per cent to 158.395 per dollar.

Oct 13 : Anthropic asked a US appeals court on Tuesday to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon's decision to label the AI company as a national security supply chain risk over a dispute about safety guardrails on its technology. • A federal appeals court in September upheld the designation in a 2-1 decision, agreeing with the Pentagon that the firm's safety restrictions could compromise military operations. SYDNEY, Oct 14 : Commonwealth Bank of Australia CEO Matt Comyn said on Wednesday Australia must ensure more of the economic benefits created by AI remain in the country while regulation should work to build trust in the new technology.   Comyn said CBA, Australia's largest lender, is rolling out AI technologies across its banking portfolio, especially in business banking. The bank has also launched an AI chat within its banking app to selected customers that can access personal and business banking details. Comyn said AI could be the "most significant technology shift we have seen" but warned an official framework was needed as the technology rolls out at a fast pace around the world.

"Realising the AI opportunity will require regulation to keep pace," he said at the bank's annual investor meeting in Sydney. "Effective regulation should help build trust in AI while ensuring global technology companies operate in accordance with Australian laws and standards, and that more of the economic value created by AI is captured in Australia." Australia has started to toughen its approach to AI regulation after initially giving an unconditional welcome to AI companies.  The Labor government has responded to community pushback against AI and data centre development by saying it would take a tougher approach. The government has said it is preparing a wide-ranging set of AI laws to take effect from early 2027, which would include limits to water and energy use by data centres, as well as copyright protections and cybersecurity measures. Comyn said Australia's economy remained resilient, although more frequent and volatile international shocks were likely. "It will take time for higher interest rates to bring inflation back into the target range," Comyn said. The remarks come a day after minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's September meeting showed the board remained concerned about persistent inflation pressures and considered further rate hikes could be needed if price growth proved more stubborn than expected.  The central bank last month ordered a fourth interest rate rise for the year which took the official cash rate to 4.6 per cent, the highest level in 15 years. Comyn said Australia had little control over external shocks and would need to boost productivity through measures including building more homes, delivering reliable low-cost energy at scale and adopting technologies such as AI across the economy. In his address to shareholders, CBA Chair Paul O'Malley said cost-of-living pressures and higher interest rates continued to affect households unevenly, while businesses were managing elevated input costs and supply uncertainty. Succession planning remained a focus for the lender, O'Malley said, a year after telling shareholders Comyn would remain in the CEO role for at least another three years.
